02 / ORIENTATION

The person behind
the projects

I'm interested in difficult problems — particularly the ones that sit between disciplines.

A high-school student from Kolkata working across science, technology, research, entrepreneurship, education and youth leadership.

FOUNDER · UNITEED

Areeb Rabbani is the Founder and President of UniteEd, a student-led NGO working to make STEM education accessible to more children. A Class 10 student at La Martiniere for Boys, Kolkata, he is also Co-Founder and Editor-in-Chief of The Luminary Journal, an international student science publication, and helped host the biggest teen-led youth summit in India.

He is a winner of the Asian Rounds of the Space Settlement Design Competition and of the International HAX Robotics Competition, a Silver Certificate awardee at the TeenTech National Awards, an Outstanding Delegate and Special Mention at international and national MUNs, and on the core committee of his school's Social Media Club.

THE WIDER WORLD

0 / THE YEAR IT SHIFTED

The year
it shifted

A few hours in May changed what normal looks like. This is the part that isn't on the résumé.

MAY 2026 · RESULTS DAY

My father is in politics, and the 2026 West Bengal election results were the day my family's world turned over. He won his own seat, but his party lost power for the first time in fifteen years. I watched it on a screen with my whole family in one room. By the afternoon, people I had never seen cry were crying, and I understood we were about to lose the life we'd had. I cried for about two hours, harder than I had in years.

THE WEEK AFTER

Within days we were given notice to move out of the house I'd lived in for nine years. We packed every gift, trophy, toy and souvenir into brown boxes and sent them somewhere I couldn't reach. On the last night I didn't cry. I kept working until the final minute, said goodbye, got in the car and fell asleep.

FIVE MONTHS IN ONE ROOM

We went from a house with five bedrooms to a single room, shared by the three of us, with family visiting when they could. Two parents who had lost the work that defined them, and who, out of fear for my future, wanted to watch every hour of mine. I used to go two days without a real conversation with them. Now there was nowhere to go. I had to run an NGO, a journal and a summit from the corner of one room.

THE SLUMP

I had my best MUN result yet at LMUN, then walked into the hardest committee at XMUN and left with a Special Mention while my classmates took Outstanding Delegate. After that the wins dried up. My schoolwork got sloppy, the journal stalled, and I lost more competitions. For the first time since Class 8, I felt like a nobody again.

WHAT HELD

UniteEd kept growing. Crucible of Dreams reached 120+ kids and brought in 40+ members and three collaborations. Voice of Youth ended as a giant success. Those two things were the proof, to me, that the building hadn't stopped.

I lost a house. I didn't lose the habit of building.

0 / THE UNFILTERED PART

What it
costs

Everything above is the highlight reel. This is the rest of it.

I'd rather you hear it from me than assume the profile is as smooth as it looks.

01TOO MANY THINGS AT ONCE

An NGO, a journal, a summit, a club, MUN and ICSE Class 10, all running together. I start more than I can carry, and the real cost is the thing that slips quietly when attention is somewhere else.

02THINGS I BUILT THAT SLOWED DOWN

Orion Accords is paused. The Luminary Journal went through a hiatus. Ambition moves faster than a volunteer team does, and I've had to learn that launching something and sustaining it are two different skills.

03THE LONGER LIST OF ATTEMPTS

Not every submission lands. The fall cycle at the Harvard International Review ended with no award. Every list of wins hides a longer list of tries, and I'm still learning to treat a no as data.

04THE TECHNICAL GAP

I can lead a team to build a thing before I can build all of it myself. Python and AI are still developing, and that bothers me enough that I'm closing it on purpose, through CS50 and real projects.

05CONTROL VS. REST

I want full control over how I spend every hour, and I also need permission to just stop for a night. Those two fight each other. Most of my growth this year has been learning when the off switch is the productive choice.

06NO MAP FOR THIS PATH

I'm choosing research, building and an international route over the JEE/NEET road in a system designed around it. That means fewer people to copy and no clear template to follow, so I make my own.

FEWER, FINISHED

Fewer things, done properly, beat many things half-alive.

BUILD IT MYSELF

Close the technical gap so I'm not only on the strategy side.

PROTECT THE OFF SWITCH

Rest isn't the opposite of ambition. It's what makes it last.

0 / THE OBSESSION

The college
obsession

I want MIT, Harvard, Stanford and Caltech. Badly. I'm not going to pretend I don't.

It isn't the name on the sweatshirt. It's that each of these places is full of the kind of people I want to be surrounded by, working on the kind of problems I can't stop thinking about.

MIT

WHERE BUILDING IS THE CULTURE

Mind and hand. The place where an idea becomes a prototype by default, and the closest match to how I already work.

Caltech

SMALL, SHARP, CLOSEST TO SPACE

Research-first and tiny enough that nobody hides, with JPL down the road. The most direct line to the space work I care about.

Stanford

WHERE FOUNDERS GET MADE

Science and startups sharing a campus, the best place I know to turn research into something that scales.

Harvard

IDEAS, WRITING, DIPLOMACY

The MUN, essay and science-communication side of me. A place to sharpen how I argue, not only what I build.

The part I keep reminding myself of: acceptance rates at these schools are brutally low, and nothing I do guarantees an outcome. So I'm not building a profile to get in. I'm building things that exist whether or not the letter comes, and trusting the story is already true by the time I apply.

THE PLAN, NOT THE PRAYER

SAT in Class 11→2 APs in Class 11→3 APs in Class 12→Capstone + paper→The big event→Essays

THE RISK I'M TAKING · ALL IN ON BUILDING, NOT ON ONE ADMISSIONS LETTER
